decisions.reason: As a flagship reusable crate in a core application area, it closely fits the firm's existing packaging knowledge and gives strong scope for learning and refinement rather than withdrawal.
A foldable large container builds directly on the firm's established container engineering and was given visible market support, so management would be likely to improve and retain it.

A stackable plastic crate is highly related to the firm's core capabilities, and even with modest early visibility the firm would usually keep such a line long enough to absorb customer feedback and optimize it.
A medium-duty rackable pallet sits squarely within the firm's pallet and logistics expertise, making it a product the firm can readily interpret, adapt and commercialize further.

Although somewhat more specialized than standard transport packaging, the spill-retention pallet still draws on adjacent pallet know-how and a dedicated launch presence suggests the firm will try to develop the niche before exiting.
This plastic pallet variant is closely related to the firm's existing pallet platform and should benefit from incremental engineering improvements, so dropping it after only a year would be unlikely.
